transcript.content: Hello, welcome in — I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Um, yeah—thanks. I guess I’m here because this thing at work has been, you know, sitting in my head for a long time. I’m a composer—music director, sometimes, depending on the project—and after this commission I did, almost two years ago now, I started noticing things in the ensemble.

Like schedule changes that didn’t make sense, seating decisions, small comments in rehearsals that sounded casual but weren’t really casual. It felt like a few people were quietly trying to undermine the work, or me, I guess. And I know people show me emails or rehearsal notes that supposedly explain it, and I’ll read them, but it doesn’t… it doesn’t change what I’m seeing.

Sorry, I’m probably not explaining it cleanly. Rehearsals are already chaotic—coffee cups on stands, everyone tuning at the same time, someone always late because parking is impossible—but this was different. It’s been almost two years and I still can’t shake the certainty of it.
Aside from these beliefs about being undermined, have you ever heard, seen, or sensed things that other people around you didn't seem to notice—like voices or sounds that weren't there?

I don’t think so. I mean, not like… voices talking to me or anything like that. Sometimes in rehearsal I’ll hear a weird overtone or someone’s chair squeak and I’ll think, wait, where did that come from—but that’s just what rooms are like, especially bad rehearsal rooms with fluorescent lights and those metal stands that rattle if you breathe near them.

So, no, I haven’t really noticed things other people couldn’t hear or see. It’s more about what people do, the timing of things, the little decisions that don’t add up.

Outside of this situation at work, would you say you've generally had a hard time trusting people—friends, family, other collaborators—going back to when you were younger, like in your teens or twenties, even before this commission happened?

I don’t know—trusting people generally? I mean, I’ve always been a little… selective, I guess. Not in some dramatic way. In grad school you kind of learn to be careful who you show sketches to, because someone will say, “Oh, interesting texture,” and then two weeks later there’s suddenly a very similar thing in their piece, but also that could just be because everyone was listening to the same recordings that semester.

With friends and family, I don’t think I’d say I had a big problem. I had normal stuff, like wondering if someone was annoyed with me, or if I’d said the wrong thing. I don’t know if that counts as “hard time trusting.” Before the commission, I wasn’t walking around thinking everyone was against me or anything. It was more… regular caution, I suppose.
Aside from your concerns about being undermined, has this experience affected your ability to compose, complete projects, or work with other musicians and collaborators over the past two years?

Yeah, it has affected it some. Not like I stopped composing or couldn’t finish anything. I still get the work done, and I haven’t lost jobs over it, at least not directly. I’m still functioning, paying rent, making coffee at stupid hours, answering messages—normal stuff.

But rehearsals take more out of me now. I’ll find myself watching decisions really closely, like why that player got moved or why the order changed, and then I’m tired before we’ve even gotten through the first run. Emails too—I reread them a lot, sometimes too many times, and I’ll ask for clarification when maybe another person would just let it go. It’s just hard not to check the seams, if that makes sense.

So… yes, it takes more energy, especially with collaborators, but I haven’t stopped working or taking care of myself.

During this past two years, have you gone through any stretches of feeling persistently very low, hopeless, or uninterested in things—or on the flip side, unusually elevated, energetic, or needing much less sleep than usual?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. I mean, there are definitely days where I feel worn down or discouraged, especially after rehearsals or after reading some email that’s worded in this very… careful institutional way. You know, like when people say “just circling back” and somehow it sounds like a threat, even though maybe it’s just office language.

But persistently low or hopeless? I don’t think so. And I don’t think I’ve had the other thing either—like suddenly feeling amazing and not needing sleep. My sleep gets weird when I’m working close to a deadline, but that’s kind of composer life. You stay up adjusting one measure because the bass clarinet entrance feels wrong, and then suddenly it’s 3 a.m.

So… no, I haven’t really noticed stretches like that. More stress and frustration than anything.

When people offer explanations or evidence that contradicts what you're sensing about being undermined, is there any part of you that considers they might be right, or does it always feel certain to you that something is going on?

I mean… I try to consider it. I do. If someone sends me an email saying, “No, the seating change was because of sightlines,” or “the schedule moved because the room wasn’t available,” there’s a part of me that can understand those words as an explanation.

But it doesn’t really settle it. Not for long. Because then I’m back in the rehearsal and someone makes one of those small comments, or there’s another little adjustment, and it all fits the same pattern again. It’s hard to explain without sounding like I’m making a whole conspiracy out of chairs and calendar invites, but after the commission it really did feel like a few people started using those small things to undercut the piece.

So… I wouldn’t say I never hear the other side. I hear it. I can repeat it back. But I don’t really believe it, most of the time. It still feels like something is going on.
